content: 1. On September 28, 2017, a press release was accessed regarding a high-level meeting on antimicrobial resistance. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) published the fifth revision of the document titled Critically Important Antimicrobials for Human Medicine in 2017. This document was accessed on September 28, 2017, and is available on the WHO website. 3. In October 2017, the Tripartite organizations, including the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), and the World Health Organization (WHO), reaffirmed their commitment to providing multi-sectoral and collaborative leadership in addressing global health challenges. This document was accessed on October 27, 2017. 4. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) approach provides a structured pathway for evaluating the quality of evidence. This methodology is detailed on the Cochrane Training website and was accessed on September 28, 2017. 5. A WHO working group consultation held in Canberra, Australia, from February 15–18, 2005, produced a report on Critically Important Antibacterial Agents for Human Medicine for Risk Management Strategies of Non-Human Use. This report is available on the WHO IRIS platform and was accessed on August 4, 2017. 6. The WHO guidelines on the use of medically important antimicrobials in food-producing animals emphasize several recommendations, including reducing overall antimicrobial use, restricting use for growth promotion, and limiting preventive use in the absence of disease. 7. In cases where disease is present, antimicrobials should be used for control and treatment purposes. The guidelines categorize antimicrobials based on their importance to human medicine, with classifications such as Critically Important, Highly Important, and Important. 8. Complete restriction of certain antimicrobials is recommended unless a veterinary professional, familiar with the disease history of the herd, determines that there is a high risk of contracting a specific infectious disease. 9. When antimicrobials are used, the selection should prioritize agents that are of the least importance to human medicine to minimize the risk of antimicrobial resistance.
